title: John Dalton and the Discovery of Color Blindness (1794)
explainer: In 1794 the English chemist John Dalton gave the first scientific account of color blindness, describing his own inability to distinguish red from green; the condition is still called 'Daltonism' in some languages in his honor. Human color vision runs on three types of cone cells, and a meaningful share of people (overwhelmingly men, due to the genes involved) have cones that overlap or are missing, which is exactly why relying on color alone - a red error state versus a green success state - locks some users out of information everyone else gets for free.

title: Jim Thatcher and the First PC Screen Reader (1986)
explainer: Blind computer scientist Jim Thatcher built some of the first software that let a blind person use a personal computer by speech, developing an early IBM screen-access program around 1986 that laid the groundwork for IBM Screen Reader - one of the first widely used tools translating what's on a PC's screen into speech output. That decades-old problem, making an interface's content available to someone who cannot see the screen, is exactly what semantic labels, focus order, and accessibility APIs in modern native apps exist to solve.
